claims.text: CoCrFeMnNi is an equiatomic quinary alloy that can have a single-phase FCC structure.
The proposed initial material is annealed to remove residual stresses and has a micrometer-scale grain size.
Plastic deformation from cryogenic to ambient temperature may involve dislocation glide together with deformation-induced nanotwinning or FCC-to-HCP martensitic transformation.
The relative contributions of glide, twinning, and martensitic transformation depend on composition, processing history, and testing conditions.
Dislocation cell structures and occasional nanotwins can form during tensile deformation of single-phase FCC CoCrFeMnNi.
Deformation-induced HCP martensite may form in CoCrFeMnNi under tension.
At temperatures above approximately 800 K, diffusion-assisted dislocation climb may become active.
Grain-boundary sliding may contribute to high-temperature deformation above approximately 800 K.
The dominant deformation mode changes from dislocation glide near 800 K to diffusion-controlled dislocation creep near 1000 K.
Yield strength increases as temperature decreases, particularly into the cryogenic range.
The low-temperature increase in yield strength is caused by dislocation glide, nanotwinning, or martensitic transformation.
Deformation-induced nanotwinning can delay necking, sustain work hardening, and increase cryogenic ductility.
FCC-to-HCP transformation can produce enhanced strength or ductility in CoCrFeMnNi.
Conventional FCC alloys such as pure Ni and Fe-Ni alloys primarily deform by dislocation glide and have moderate strain-rate sensitivity.
The hypothesis is restricted to single-phase FCC equiatomic quinary alloys and may not generalize to multiphase alloys.
The hypothesis may not hold for BCC alloys or nanocrystalline materials dominated by grain-boundary mechanisms.
High-temperature strain-rate insensitivity depends on grain size and precipitate distribution.
Strong strain-rate dependence of yield strength at 900 K would falsify the proposed diffusion-controlled mechanism.
Absence of both FCC-to-HCP transformation and nanotwinning at 77 K despite high work hardening would falsify the proposed twinning-or-martensite competition.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis repeatedly states that the high-temperature relationship between yield strength and strain rate is unclear, yet the falsification experiment treats strong strain-rate dependence at 900 K as decisively incompatible with diffusion-controlled deformation, implicitly predicting weak or absent rate dependence.
